title: Shloka Compiler
abstract: This document specifies the six transformations that carry a Sanskrit verse to an executable rule, and states what each one preserves and what it loses §1 . It argues that translation is a validation artefact generated from the analysis rather than a stage in the compilation path §3 , that anuvṛtti resolution is exactly scope resolution and cross-reference resolution is exactly linking — in both cases unresolved references are errors, not warnings §5.2, §6.2 — and that unresolved ambiguity is a first-class compiler output emitted for scholar adjudication rather than guessed at §1.1, §7 . sections.heading: Abstract
sections.html:
This document specifies the six transformations that carry a Sanskrit verse to an executable rule, and states what each one preserves and what it loses (§1). It argues that translation is a validation artefact generated from the analysis rather than a stage in the compilation path (§3), that anuvṛtti resolution is exactly scope resolution and cross-reference resolution is exactly linking — in both cases unresolved references are errors, not warnings (§5.2, §6.2) — and that unresolved ambiguity is a first-class compiler output emitted for scholar adjudication rather than guessed at (§1.1, §7).

The source document is marked Status: Draft for review and is published here as an Active research document: drafted, but not accepted as specification. The document-level statement of that condition is made by choir/research/README.md: "All 18 deliverables drafted. None accepted. Every document is a hypothesis, per MANIFESTO.md." MANIFESTO.md itself states the rule at the level of objects rather than documents: "Treat every computational object as a hypothesis rather than an established truth."

sections.heading: Research Question
sections.html:
The source states its own framing at §1: "The brief specifies the pipeline to be researched: Shloka → Translation → Grammar → Meaning → Reasoning → Computational Graph → Executable Rule. Each arrow is a transformation with its own inputs, outputs, failure modes, and information loss. This document specifies all six and states what is preserved across each."

A second question is embedded in the framing and is answered against the brief rather than with it: whether translation belongs in that chain at all (§3).

sections.heading: Finding
sections.html:
The compiler analogy is load-bearing, and it breaks in exactly one place

The document states that "the compiler analogy is used seriously, not decoratively," on the ground that "every stage has a genuine counterpart in conventional compilation, and the correspondence is load-bearing: it tells us what the hard problems are and where the established solutions live" (§1). The correspondence table it gives:

Shloka compiler stageConventional compilerWhat transfers
Normalisation + sandhi splittingLexical analysisTokenisation; but here it is ambiguous
Morphology + compounds + parseSyntactic analysisParse forests, not parse trees
Kāraka + sense resolutionSemantic analysisType checking against the ontology
Anuvṛtti resolutionName binding / scope resolutionExact analogy; free variables must bind
Frame → HIRIR generationLowering
Normalisation, dedupOptimisationCanonicalisation
Cross-reference resolutionLinkingUnresolved references are errors
MIR → LIRCode generationTarget-specific lowering

Two of these are called exact — scope resolution and linking — and the document says they "are the ones that catch the errors most likely to produce silently wrong rules" (§1).

The analogy is stated to break in one place, and the break is not treatable by engineering: "A conventional compiler's source language is unambiguous by construction. Ours is not, and no amount of engineering will make it so" (§1.1). The consequence is stated as a governing property:

CHOIR is a compiler whose front end cannot always decide, and whose correct behaviour in that case is to emit a diagnostic rather than a guess. (§1.1)

This makes the shloka compiler "an interactive compiler with a human adjudication gate," and makes "ambiguity a first-class output rather than an internal difficulty" (§1.1).

Stage A — Shloka → Attested Text

The document adds a stage the brief's chain leaves implicit, "and it is where most downstream errors originate" (§2). Input is a verse as encountered; output is an attested textual object with full provenance. Operations: script normalisation (SLP1 internal, IAST display, citing 005 §3); locus assignment per edition, "since numbering varies"; edition capture; variant collection as parallel branches; and attestation grading, ordered "critical edition > printed edition > digital corpus > quotation."

The named failure mode is the unattested quotation: "A verse circulating in secondary literature without an edition reference is extremely common and is the dominant source of citation error." Such text is admitted with attestation: unverified and "is barred from the authoritative corpus until checked" (§2). Information preserved at this stage: "everything. This stage is purely additive."

Stage B — translation is removed from the compilation path

The document qualifies the brief in a way it says "changes the architecture":

Translation is a validation artefact, not a compilation stage. (§3)

The reason given is information loss: "Compiling through a translation loses the grammatical structure that Stage C depends on — case, voice, mood, compound type. English cannot carry the ablative-as-reference-frame distinction that carries requirement R10" (§3). The dependency is therefore inverted — grammar and meaning are computed from the text, and translation is generated from the analysis so a reviewer can check the analysis. That check is the round-trip test of §8.2, which the document says "is far more useful than translation-first."

One exception is recorded: texts with no reliable Sanskrit source. A translation-only path exists, produces rules flagged derivation: translation-only, and "carries a hard confidence ceiling because the grammatical justification chain is absent." The document explicitly leaves open "whether such rules enter the authoritative corpus at all," citing 005 §12.3 (§3).

Existing translations "are used as evidence, not as input": agreement across translations on conditional structure raises interpretive confidence, disagreement flags the verse for review, and "translation divergence is one of the better automated signals for 'this verse is contested'" (§3).

Stage C — Text → Grammar

This stage is "the pipeline S0–S6 of sanskrit_analysis_pipeline.md, entire" (§4). Its output is "a forest of kāraka-labelled dependency analyses with scores" — not a single parse. Information preserved is "the full lattice, with pruning decisions recorded," and every surviving analysis "retains character-offset spans into the source, so any downstream object can point back at the exact substring it came from." The document states that "this span-preservation is what makes the traceability invariant reach all the way to the manuscript" (§4).

Failure modes are deferred to 005 §9 in full, with three named as silent: "ablative/genitive syncretism, bahuvrīhi misclassification, and undetected elision" (§4).

Stage D — Grammar → Meaning

Three operations in order (§5).

Symbol resolution is deliberately restricted. Sanskrit technical terms resolve against domain namespaces (guru → choir:jyotisha/graha/Guru rather than choir:jyotisha/social/Guru), "**But polysemy internal to the domain is not resolved here.**" Following vedic_reasoning_methodology.md §3.1, "when the rule concludes something about Sūrya, the question of whether that means father, bone or authority is answered by the query's purpose, at execution time. Resolving it at compile time would bake one reading into the corpus and make it answer only one kind of question" (§5.1). The split is stated as:

Compile-time resolution: which entity. Run-time resolution: which signification of that entity. (§5.1)

***Anuvṛtti resolution is scope binding* — stage S7 of the Sanskrit pipeline, "and the exact analogue of name binding" (§5.2). The worked illustration is a section head establishing scope ("In the matter of natal charts, reckoned from the Ascendant…") and a verse that overrides the reference frame locally (candrāt) while inheriting the application (jātaka): "…Jupiter in a kendra from the Moon yields Gajakesarī." The rule is unconditional: "Unbound free variables are compile errors. A rule whose subject or scope is unresolved does not enter the corpus. Emitting it with a guessed default is the single most damaging thing this compiler could do, because the result is a well-formed over-general rule that fires where it should not."

Modality detection maps optative/gerundive morphology to injunctive force, feeding the vidhi / arthavāda gate of vedic_reasoning_methodology.md §4.3. "Non-injunctive verses are classified and stored, but not compiled to rules. They remain available as context and as commentarial evidence" (§5.3).

The document marks this stage as the point where "Information loss begins": metre is dropped (recorded, not carried), poetic figures are noted but not modelled, word order is normalised. "All are retained in the source mapping and none affect rule semantics — this is the first deliberate loss and it is documented as such" (§5.3).

Stage E — Meaning → Reasoning

The step that identifies antecedent, consequent, and what modifies the link (§6). Structural decomposition is given as:

ElementGrammatical signalExample marker
ConditionConditional particle; locative absolute; relative clausecet, yadi, yadā; locative absolute
ConclusionMain clause; optative verbbhavet, syāt
Scope restrictionAdverbial; scope-limiting compoundjātake, divā
ExceptionAdversative particle; negated conditiontu, kintu, na tu
Strength qualifierAdjective on the conclusion; degree termpūrṇa, alpa
Named resultnāmadheya constructionnāma, saṃjñā

The document names a hazard here: "Sanskrit's conditional constructions are various and frequently implicit — a locative absolute carries conditional force with no overt particle at all… a verse can be a conditional rule without containing anything a keyword search would find." Recognising implicit conditionals "requires the dependency parse, which is one of the arguments for not compiling through translation" (§6.1).

Cross-reference resolution is linking (§6.2), with four stated properties: unresolved references are errors, not warnings; references resolve against a versioned corpus, so a rule records which version of e.g. the kendra definition it was compiled against; circular definitions are detected and rejected; and the dependency graph "is what enables incremental recompilation when a definition changes."

Exceptions default to undercutting (§6.3), typed per computational_primitives.md §3.12. "A cancellation clause in śāstra almost never asserts the opposite conclusion; it withdraws the rule. Typing an exception as rebutting requires positive textual evidence that the opposite is asserted. Getting this default backwards manufactures conclusions the corpus never made." The document also concedes a limit it cannot engineer away: exceptions "are frequently in different verses, sometimes different chapters, and occasionally different texts. The compiler cannot always know it has found them all — which is why exception_completeness is tracked as a distinct confidence input (confidence_framework.md §3.2) rather than assumed."

Stage F — Reasoning → Computational Graph (HIR)

Emission into the high-level IR specified in choir_intermediate_representation.md §3. "The distinguishing property: HIR represents unresolved ambiguity explicitly." The recorded shape:

Ambiguity {
  id, span,                      # where in the source
  kind: segmentation | compound_type | sense | attachment | scope,
  alternatives: [ { reading, score, consequence } ],
  status: open | resolved | contested,
  resolution: { chosen, by, grounds, timestamp }?
}

"Every downstream object that depends on an open ambiguity inherits a reference to it. A rule with open ambiguities can still be inspected, discussed, and counted — it simply cannot be executed until they are closed." The document states this "is the structural difference from a conventional compiler, and it is why HIR is a distinct layer rather than an implementation detail" (§7).

The adjudication loop runs compile → ambiguity diagnostics → scholar review → recorded resolution → resolution cache, which is then "reused automatically on structurally identical cases" (§7.1). The document emphasises the cache on the grounds that "śāstric verse is formulaic: the same constructions recur across hundreds of verses. A resolution recorded once — 'in this construction, candrāt is apādāna, not genitive' — applies automatically to every structurally identical instance thereafter, with provenance naming the original adjudication. The scholar's cost is front-loaded and amortised." Cached resolutions "are themselves versioned and revisable. Revising one invalidates and recompiles everything that used it."

Stage G — Graph → Executable Rule

HIR → MIR → LIR, per choir_intermediate_representation.md §§4–5.

LoweringOperationLosesPreserves
HIR → MIRResolve ambiguities; canonicalise; normalise; dedupRejected alternatives (moved to provenance)Source spans; all semantics
MIR → LIRIndex; compile match patterns; order for executionNothing semanticEverything, plus back-pointers

"MIR is the interchange layer — domain-independent, fully resolved, canonical. It is what domain_independence.md tests portability against, and what a legal or clinical front end would also target" (§8.1). Canonicalisation "is what makes content addressing work (reasoning_ontology.md §7.2): two verses stating the same rule normalise to the same MIR, hash identically, and unify — producing one rule with two independent attestations. That is a genuine evidential signal obtained for free from the identity scheme."

The round-trip test is the compiler's primary self-check (§8.2): compile the shloka to a rule, decompile the rule to a paraphrase, compare the paraphrase to the original. The document is explicit that "this is a fidelity test, not an equivalence test — the paraphrase will not be the verse — and it is scored by human review against a rubric":

CriterionQuestion
Condition fidelityAre the antecedents the same, with the same scope?
Conclusion fidelityIs the consequent the same, with the same strength and modality?
Exception fidelityAre all exceptions present and correctly typed?
Scope fidelitySame context, same reference frame?
No additionDoes the rule assert anything the verse does not?

The last criterion "is the one that catches the worst failures. Over-generation is more dangerous than under-generation: a missing rule is a gap; an invented rule is a falsehood with a citation attached" (§8.2).

Diagnostics

The taxonomy is "modelled on compiler error levels, because the severity distinctions are the same" (§9).

LevelMeaningCorpus admission
FatalCannot proceedRejected
ErrorStructurally incompleteRejected until fixed
AmbiguityMultiple readings; needs adjudicationHeld, not executable
WarningCompiles, but suspiciousAdmitted, flagged
NoteInformationalAdmitted
CodeLevelCondition
E-ATTESTErrorNo verifiable edition
E-SEGErrorNo valid segmentation
E-BINDErrorUnresolved free variable (anuvṛtti failure)
E-LINKErrorUnresolved cross-reference
E-CYCLEFatalCircular definition
A-SEGAmbiguityMultiple coherent segmentations
A-CMPDAmbiguityCompound type undetermined
A-SCOPEAmbiguityMultiple candidate scope bindings
A-SENSEAmbiguityUnresolved lexical sense
W-ARTHAWarningMay be arthavāda; injunctive force uncertain
W-EXCWarningException set may be incomplete
W-TRANSWarningTranslation-only derivation
W-VARIANTWarningMeaning depends on a contested reading
N-DEDUPNoteUnified with an existing rule (independent attestation)

The document records that "W-ARTHA and W-EXC are the two warnings that most often indicate a real problem, and both resist automation — they are the natural focus of scholar review time" (§9).

Confidence propagation

Each stage contributes to extraction confidence per confidence_framework.md §3.1, and "the composition rule is deliberately pessimistic":

Stage confidences do not multiply. Extraction confidence is bounded by the minimum stage confidence, then reduced further for open ambiguities. (§10)

Two reasons are given against multiplication: "stage confidences are not independent (a bad segmentation causes a bad parse), and multiplication of many high values produces a misleadingly low result while a single catastrophic stage failure gets diluted. A chain is as strong as its weakest link, and this one is literally a chain." The stated formula:

extraction_confidence = min(stage_confidences) × ambiguity_penalty(open_count)
                      × attestation_factor(source_grade)

"Human adjudication raises the relevant stage confidence, with the adjudication recorded — so a scholar-resolved ambiguity is not merely closed, it is closed by someone, on the record" (§10).

sections.heading: Architectural Implications
sections.html:
The compilation chain is Text → Grammar → Meaning → Reasoning → HIR → MIR → LIR, with translation outside it (§3, §12). The source frames this as a qualification to the brief — "Translation is a validation artefact, not a compilation stage" — rather than as a conformance rule for implementers. What it does state is that translations enter as generated review artefacts and as evidence, and that translation-only derivations carry the W-TRANS warning and a hard confidence ceiling.

Ambiguity must be representable in the IR, not merely handled in the front end. Because HIR carries explicit Ambiguity records and downstream objects inherit references to open ones, the executability gate is structural: a rule with open ambiguities is inspectable, discussable and countable but not executable (§7). This is the source's stated reason for HIR being a distinct layer rather than an implementation detail.

Two error classes are hard rejections rather than degradations. Unbound anuvṛtti variables (E-BIND) and unresolved cross-references (E-LINK) keep a rule out of the corpus (§5.2, §6.2); circular definitions (E-CYCLE) are fatal. The document's justification is that the failure mode of guessing is a well-formed over-general rule, which is worse than absence.

Symbolic interpretation is deferred to execution time. Compile-time resolves which entity; run-time resolves which signification (§5.1). A corpus that resolved symbolism early would, per the source, "answer only one kind of question."

Versioning and incremental recompilation are required, not optional. Rules record the corpus version of every definition they link against, cached resolutions are versioned and revisable, and revising one "invalidates and recompiles everything that used it" (§6.2, §7.1).

MIR is the portability contract. It is the layer domain_independence.md tests against and the target a legal or clinical front end would also emit to (§8.1); canonicalisation at MIR is what makes content addressing and independent-attestation unification work (reasoning_ontology.md §7.2).

Throughput may be bounded by scholar availability. The adjudication gate, the human-scored round-trip rubric, and the two hand-reviewed warnings all place scholars on the critical path; the source raises this as an open planning constraint rather than a solved one, conditional on Stage E not being automatable (§11, open questions 1 and 4).

sections.heading: Open Questions
sections.html:
The source records five (§11), reproduced with its own hedges:

  1. Can Stage E be automated at all? "Identifying antecedent/consequent structure in metrically-reordered verse with implicit conditionals may be irreducibly interpretive. If it is not automatable, throughput is bounded by scholar availability and the project should be planned around that."
  2. Resolution cache generalisation. "Structural identity is safe. Structural similarity would generalise much further but risks propagating an error across hundreds of rules. Where the line sits is unresolved and consequential."
  3. Cross-text linking. Exceptions stated in a different text raise a question "the compiler cannot answer alone: is that text authoritative for this one? This is a source-authority question (conflict_resolution.md §5.3), not a compilation question, but it blocks linking."
  4. Round-trip scoring cost. The round-trip test "requires human review per rule, which does not scale. Whether an automated paraphrase-similarity proxy is trustworthy enough for triage — given the neural/symbolic boundary in knowledge_graph_spec.md §2.5 — is open. Note that using it for triage of review effort does not violate that boundary; using it as a fidelity score would."
  5. Incremental recompilation scope. "Revising a cached resolution or a definition invalidates dependents transitively. Whether the blast radius is manageable at corpus scale is unknown."

Two further items are left unresolved outside §11: whether translation-only rules enter the authoritative corpus at all (§3, deferred to 005 §12.3), and the source's own status — it is marked "Draft for review," and no acceptance is recorded.

  • YK-R-004 — Vedic Reasoning Methodology — supplies the run-time symbolism rule (§3.1) and the vidhi / arthavāda gate (§4.3).
